newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Britain, UAE to sign defence pact.
newsitem.headline: Britain, UAE to sign defence pact.

text.p: Britain and the United Arab Emirates are due to sign a defence cooperation pact on Thursday that British arms manufacturers hope will pave the way for more business in the Gulf.
British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo will hold talks in the UAE capital Abu Dhabi with senior sheikhs of the oil-rich emirate, one of the richest states in the volatile region.
He is due to meet the UAE's armed forces chief of staff, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zaid al-Nahayan, and minister of state for foreign affairs Sheikh Hamdan bin Zaid.
They are sons of the UAE federation's veteran president Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan, who will lead national celebrations next Monday for the country's silver jubilee.

The UAE was formed in 1971 when Britain withdrew its protection from the Gulf's Trucial States -- Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ras al-Khaimah, Umm al-Qawwain, Ajman and Fujairah -- which it had ruled and defended for 150 years.
The defence pact was delayed by years of bargaining over such sticking points as jurisdiction over British troops operating in UAE territory.
Diplomats and UAE officials said the pact was due to be signed by Portillo and Sheikh Hamdan.
The UAE has defence pacts with the United States and France that have helped lead to military contracts worth more than $4.3 billion in the last three years.

The UAE wants all its defence agreements to be on the lines of the one it signed last December with France, which pledges Paris to rush 70,000 rapid reaction force troops and air power to the region if the sparsely populated and militarily vulnerable country is threatened.
Britain's military presence in the Gulf is low-key -- one frigate serves as the Armilla Patrol which began in October 1980.
The United States usually has at least 20 warships in the area, including a carrier battle group, as part of the Gulf-based U.S. Fifth Fleet.
British officers have been seconded to the UAE armed forces, largely in training roles.
